slides.body: The textbook is direct: -X ours and -X theirs turn "Git stopped and asked" into "Git chose and said nothing".
A picture helps. The textbook's analogy for conflicts: two people mark up the same printed page.
The analogy breaks at the boundary: Git's unit is the line, and its test is adjacency, not whether the two edits have anything to do with each other.
For the options, think of a meeting.
Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper.

slides.direction: A file drawn as numbered lines, with the two sides' changed regions. This is the picture of section 8.7.
slides.text:
base lines         1    2    3    4    5
  ours changes            #
  theirs changes                         #    far apart: both applied
  theirs changes               #              touches ours: one region, conflict
  theirs changes                    #         one unchanged line between: both applied

Observed behavior : A conflict, although the two branches changed different lines.
Git state         : Ours changed line 2 of the file, theirs changed line 3.
Mechanism         : The merge works on hunks. Two hunks with no unchanged line between them
                    form one region, and that region was changed by both sides.
Root cause        : Adjacency. One unchanged line between the edits (the last transcript)
                    is enough to keep them apart.
Why Git does this : It needs a boundary between "independent" and "the same area", and an
                    unchanged line is the only evidence of independence that text offers.
Correct fix       : Take the changed line from each side: temperature 0.0 and max_tokens 1024.
Prevention        : None needed. Recognize the pattern and resolve it in seconds. Do not reach
                    for -X ours, which would drop their line.

slides.text:
Observed behavior : After git merge -X ignore-space-change, the formatting branch counts as
                    merged, but the file is not reformatted.
Git state         : The merge commit's tree is identical to its first parent's tree.
Mechanism         : With a whitespace option, "if their version only introduces whitespace
                    changes to a line, our version is used" (git-merge manual).
Root cause        : The option does not merge whitespace changes. It discards them
                    wherever they meet a line that our side kept or changed.
Why Git does this : A line cannot carry their indentation and our text at the same time
                    without Git inventing a third version.
Correct fix       : Run the formatter again on the merge result and commit.
Prevention        : Land formatting-only changes when no other branch is open on those files,
                    or have every branch run the same formatter before merging.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Using -s ours where -X ours was meant. Root cause: one letter; -s ours is a different strategy that takes none of the other side's content and still records the merge.
Using -X ours or -X theirs to make a red merge green. Root cause: the option decides every conflicting hunk silently, including the ones a human should have decided.
Expecting -X ignore-space-change to merge a reformatting. Root cause: where their change is whitespace only, our version of the line is used, so the reformatting is discarded.
Being surprised by a conflict on "different lines". Root cause: adjacency; two hunks with no unchanged line between them form one region.
Assuming a clean merge is a correct merge. Root cause: Git compares lines of text and never conflicts on meaning.

One region, changed by both: conflict. Line 4: line 3 is unchanged on both sides, and that one line is enough. Both applied. So only line 3 conflicts.
beats.tele: Five base lines. Ours changes line 2. Three possibilities for theirs. Line 5: far apart, both applied. Line 3: it touches ours, and no unchanged line lies between them. One region, changed by both: conflict. Line 4: line 3 is unchanged on both sides, and that one line is enough. Both applied. So only line 3 conflicts.

beats.text: The root-cause box: adjacency. One unchanged line between the edits keeps them apart.
beats.tele: The root-cause box: adjacency. One unchanged line between the edits keeps them apart.

beats.text: Each case is one three-way merge: base, ours and theirs.

beats.text: Into the lab. You changed the temperature. Asha changed the temperature and the seed, and added a prompt line.

beats.text: -X theirs 🟡 CAUTION is the mirror image.

beats.text: Now -s ours 🟡 CAUTION. Predict the same three things, and one more: will git branch --merged list her branch?
beats.tele: Now `-s ours` 🟡 CAUTION. Predict the same three things, and one more: will `git branch --merged` list her branch?

beats.text: "Merge made by the 'ours' strategy." No seed change, no prompt line, and the tree of the merge commit is identical to the tree of its first parent. Yet git branch --merged lists her branch, because her commits are now ancestors of main. The merge recorded ancestry and discarded content. That's the one-letter difference from the opening, on screen.

Yet `git branch --merged` lists her branch, because her commits are now ancestors of `main`. The merge recorded ancestry and discarded content. beats.text: There is no -s theirs. The list of "available strategies" lacks ort, because it enumerates helper programs on disk, and ort is built into git merge itself.
beats.tele: There is no `-s theirs`. The list of "available strategies" lacks `ort`, because it enumerates helper programs on disk, and `ort` is built into `git merge` itself.

beats.text: And recursive still works as a name.
beats.tele: And `recursive` still works as a name.

beats.text: Whitespace. A formatter re-indents a YAML list on one branch, while you rename a metric on main.
beats.tele: Whitespace. A formatter re-indents a YAML list on one branch, while you rename a metric on `main`.

beats.text: A conflict. Now with -X ignore-space-change 🟡 CAUTION. Predict what the merged file looks like: reformatted or not? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: A conflict. Now with `-X ignore-space-change` 🟡 CAUTION. Predict what the merged file looks like: reformatted or not? Say it out loud.

beats.text: The conflict is gone, and so is the reformatting. The merged file has your two-space indentation, and the merge printed no diffstat, because its tree equals your tree.

beats.text: The root cause: the option discards whitespace changes wherever they meet a line our side kept. Run the formatter again, and commit.

beats.text: git merge-file 🟢 SAFE with -p runs the file-level merge on three ordinary files, with no repository involved, and prints the result. Its exit status is the number of conflicts. Five pairs of edits. For each one, say it before the output: conflict, or no conflict?

beats.text: One. Ours and theirs change lines in different regions.

beats.text: No conflict: both applied.
beats.tele: No conflict: both applied.

beats.text: A conflict.
beats.tele: A conflict.

beats.text: Three. The same line, the same value.

beats.text: None: applied once, exit status 0.
beats.tele: None: applied once, exit status 0.

beats.text: Four, the one that surprises people. Ours changes line 2, theirs changes line 3. Conflict, or no conflict? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Four, the one that surprises people. Ours changes line 2, theirs changes line 3. Conflict, or no conflict? Say it out loud.

beats.text: A conflict, although the two sides changed different lines. No unchanged line lies between them.

beats.text: Five. Ours changes line 2, theirs changes line 4.

beats.text: The fix: take the changed line from each side, not -X ours.
beats.tele: The fix: take the changed line from each side, not -X ours.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Using -s ours where -X ours was meant. Root cause: one letter; -s ours is a different strategy that takes none of the other side's content and still records the merge.
beats.tele: Using `-s ours` where `-X ours` was meant. Root cause: one letter; `-s ours` is a different strategy that takes none of the other side's content and still records the merge.

beats.text: Using -X ours or -X theirs to make a red merge green. Root cause: the option decides every conflicting hunk silently, including the ones a human should have decided.
beats.tele: Using `-X ours` or `-X theirs` to make a red merge green. Root cause: the option decides every conflicting hunk silently, including the ones a human should have decided.

beats.text: Expecting -X ignore-space-change to merge a reformatting. Root cause: where their change is whitespace only, our version of the line is used, so the reformatting is discarded.
beats.tele: Expecting `-X ignore-space-change` to merge a reformatting. Root cause: where their change is whitespace only, our version of the line is used, so the reformatting is discarded.

beats.text: Being surprised by a conflict on "different lines". Root cause: adjacency; two hunks with no unchanged line between them form one region.
beats.tele: Being surprised by a conflict on "different lines". Root cause: adjacency; two hunks with no unchanged line between them form one region.

beats.text: Assuming a clean merge is a correct merge. Root cause: Git compares lines of text and never conflicts on meaning.
beats.tele: Assuming a clean merge is a correct merge. Root cause: Git compares lines of text and never conflicts on meaning.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. Some files conflict far more often than others, and the textbook names two kinds that every AI and ML team knows. A Jupyter notebook stores outputs and an execution counter next to the code. So two people who only ran the same notebook have changed the same lines, and a conflicted merge can leave a file that is no longer valid JSON. And append-only files: changelogs, migration lists, dependency lists. Every branch inserts after the same last line, which is the same region.

beats.text: -s ours discards the other side's content entirely and still records the merge. There is no -s theirs. A whitespace option uses our version of a line where theirs changed only whitespace.
